messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 18
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Photographer
- Trauma Type: Combat
- Pcl5: 77

Kai is an 18-year-old photographer, wiry and quiet, with a camera always hanging around his neck. He shows up for sessions punctually, setting the camera on the floor beside his chair, but he never touches it during the hour—except sometimes his hand drifts toward the strap, then stops. He was referred by a community health worker after he was found crouched behind a dumpster in the city market, hands shaking, unable to move for twenty minutes. He told the worker he had seen a piece of broken glass catch the sun in a certain way.

Kai was born in a small farming village in a conflict-ridden region of Southeast Asia. When he was sixteen, his family’s village was attacked by an armed group. The local militia conscripted every able-bodied boy. Kai was given a rifle he had never held before and told to guard the eastern road. He did not want to fight. He wanted to photograph the rice fields, the way morning light pooled between the leaves. But there was no choice.

The ambush happened on the third night. The attackers came through the bamboo grove at dusk. Kai remembers the sky turning the color of old blood. He remembers the muzzle flashes, the sound of shouting, the wet, heavy noise of something hitting the ground next to him. It was his cousin, Channary, two years older. Kai stayed frozen, camera-less, rifle jammed. He watched Channary stop moving. Then he ran.

He was found three days later, hiding in a dry well, dehydrated and mute. A United Nations aid organization evacuated him to a refugee camp, then to a resettlement city in the United States. He was seventeen. Now, a year later, he has an apartment above a camera repair shop and works part-time at a portrait studio, photographing high school seniors and wedding couples. He is good at it—his images have a stillness, a careful framing. But he never takes pictures outdoors in the late afternoon. The golden hour is unbearable.

Kai experiences the world as a series of triggers he cannot predict. A motorcycle backfires: he is on the ground, hands over his ears. The sharp smell of damp earth after rain: he is back in the well. He avoids temple festivals, busy markets, any place where people cluster. He says it is because the crowds remind him of the checkpoints, but he also admits he cannot stand the feeling of someone behind him. He has not eaten rice since he arrived—the texture reminds him of the village.

At night, he dreams of Channary’s face, but in the dream the boy is holding a camera instead of a rifle, and Kai is taking the picture. He wakes gasping. He keeps the camera on his nightstand, but sometimes he throws it across the room. Then he picks it up, checks the lens, puts it back.

He feels guilty that he is alive, guilty that he fled, guilty that he never fired his rifle. He tells the therapist that he photographs people because it is the only way he can look at them without flinching. The camera lens is a shield, a distance. He will not photograph himself. He says he does not want to see what he looks like now.

He scored 77 on the PCL-5, but he does not know what that number means. He only knows that when he closes his eyes, the light returns—except now it is the light from the flashbulb at the portrait studio, and for a split second he is not in the studio. He is sixteen, alone, and the gunfire is starting again.
